title: The Round-Middle Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra
author: Annotated by Master Dayou; commentated by Master Chuandeng (translated)
excerpt: Taking the retribution-body and the environment of the Land of Bliss as the wonderful being of the one-mind, and the invoking of the name as true emptiness: without true emptiness one cannot realize the wonderful being of the Land of Bliss, and without wonderful being one cannot reveal the true emptiness of this mind.

blocks.text: Preface to the Round-Middle Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra

inline.s: The Tathagata's secret speech lies in words whose meaning is manifold. It is like a king who asked for the saindhava: a single name embracing four real things. Only that wise minister understood its meaning—whether the king was about to go out, to eat, to drink, or to go to war, as soon as he uttered that one word, the minister presented him with a horse, with salt, with water, or with a vessel, never failing to grasp the king's mind and to suit his intention. The wise minister, the bodhisattva, is likewise: he well understands whatever the Tathagata teaches, expounding the shallow deeply and the deep in a shallow way, declaring what is neither shallow nor deep within that which is both shallow and deep, and what is both shallow and deep within that which is neither shallow nor deep. In composing treatises and spreading the scriptures he makes the full and the brief each fit its place—neither causing wisdom to regress nor leaving the truth deficient. Only then may he be said to have ascended the hall and entered the inner chamber. Now this Amitabha Sutra is what Shakyamuni Tathagata set forth as a shallow explanation within the deep and a brief explanation within the vast. Since the exposition was brief, the wise minister's commentary upon it could not but be brief; since the meaning is deep, his commentary could not but be deep. The brief commentary does not cause wisdom to regress, and the profound principle does not leave the truth deficient. He reaches the vast by way of the brief and takes the middle way with composure. I have seen the Brief Explanation of Master Qu'an at Wumen. Its preface says: 'The bejeweled groves and the jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source; the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature.' Again it says: 'Realizing that which is originally complete within the mind, the countless lands are not far away; knowing that the great vows may be relied upon, the three asamkhya kalpas are crossed transversely.' Alas! It gathers the whole sutra into itself, and yet its words are so very brief; it concerns the mind-nature and the self-nature, and yet its meaning is so very deep. Were it not for the bodhisattva, the wise minister, how could anyone arrive at such a point? Now I make this commentary and have entitled it specifically 'Round-Middle.' The intent is this: taking the retribution-body and the environment of the Land of Bliss as the wonderful being of the one-mind, and the invoking of the name as true emptiness. Without true emptiness one cannot realize the wonderful being of the Land of Bliss, and without wonderful being one cannot reveal the true emptiness of this mind. This is what is called the 'inconceivable provisional'—not the one-sided provisional—and 'true emptiness not empty'—not mere emptiness. Uniting these two and practicing them, the Round-Middle is rounded and complete, and the path of the 'not-merely-middle' is accomplished. Therefore it is named a commentary. My wish is that those who read this sutra and practice it may, mindful of its name, think upon its meaning. Truly they should single-mindedly remain unconfused, forgetting all deliberations, and the principle of true emptiness will be manifest. Holding the name for seven days, thought after thought continuous, the principle of wonderful being will be revealed. When the practice is complete, one sees the Buddha; when the mind is pure, the lotus opens. When the seal of Saha is broken, the text of the Land of Bliss is accomplished. The breaking of the seal is that by which feeling is emptied—this is called true emptiness; the accomplishment of the text is that by which the Dharma is established—this is called wonderful being. Both are forgotten and both are preserved. Hence the words of the Amitabha Sutra are brief and its meaning is deep. Because this commentary follows in order, I here set forth the meaning of the title, and so I write this informal preface.
Written at the time of the newly brightened moon in the last month of winter, in the first year of the dragon's ascent to the throne of the Great Ming under the Tianqi reign. Hence this preface.

blocks.text: Preface to the Brief Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha

inline.s: By the monk Dayou of Wu Commandery, Ming dynasty.

blocks.text: Next, the person who composed it.

inline.s: The master's style was Qu'an, and Dayou was his given name. He was abbot of the Beichan Tiantai Teaching Temple in Suzhou, deeply versed in doctrinal principles, and in the Pure Land path he especially grasped its subtlety. He wrote a Pure Land Compendium (Jingtu Zhigui Ji), which is now widely current in the world. His lay surname and ancestral home still await detailed verification.

Third, the explanation of the preface, in two parts. First, the reason for expounding the sutra; second, the reason for the brief annotation. The first has two parts: first, the rise of the occasion; second, the exposition of the sutra. The first in turn has two: first, the tracing of the source-stream; second, the actual account of the occasion. And the first of these has two: first, the true source is non-dual; second, the delusive streams produce distinctions.

Now when the true source is taken up, then within the one nature there is originally no distinction of suffering and joy; why then should the Tathagata appear in the world and preach a sutra? It is only because the delusive streams have produced distinctions that our Buddha manifested birth to spread the teaching. So first we make clear that the true source is non-dual.
[Commentary] Now the Still-Light is truly pure; originally there is no distinction of suffering and joy.

[Sub-commentary] 'Still-Light' is one of the four kinds of Pure Land. The four Pure Lands are: first, the Pure Land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together; second, the Pure Land of Expedient Remainder; third, the Pure Land of Real Reward and Non-obstruction; and fourth, the Pure Land of Everlasting Still-Light. Each has its pure and its impure aspect, and only the highest grade of Still-Light is the true Pure Land; the remaining Pure Lands all carry a provisional element. One must further know that the expression 'truly pure' does not mean that apart from the three lands there is some separate Still-Light to be had; it merely points to the substance of the three lower lands, whose principle is fundamentally ultimate and no different from Still-Light. Hence the Venerable Siming, in the Miaozong Chao, says: 'Know that the four lands are both horizontal and vertical, and further know that the horizontal and the vertical are only in a single place. Take the land of cohabitation: place it in one spot, and it is at once the Real Reward. One who breaks through ignorance and turns to enter that is the Dharma-body, sharing the substance and function of the Buddha and called the true, marvelous reward—even a person with purified six faculties cannot take part in it, much less a two-vehicle practitioner. This is the vertical, an instance where in one place the Real Reward is discussed. Again, if one has not broken ignorance and sees it while still in this body, this is what the Buddhas and the great bodhisattvas, for the sake of those able to see, add, causing them to see the Real Reward land. For there are those whose capacities, though not yet free of delusion, have already practiced the middle contemplation; as in the Avatamsaka assembly and other gatherings, beings of sundry types all see an inconceivable body and land. Since the Real Reward is thus, Expedient and Still-Light, in their horizontal discussion in the same place, are likewise. In the place of cohabitation one discusses the horizontal and vertical of the three lands; in the place of Expedient, the horizontal and vertical of the two lands; in the place of Real Reward, the horizontal and vertical of the one land. But at Still-Light there is neither horizontal nor vertical—even in that very place there is none. Now to say 'the Still-Light is truly pure' is to mark the true substance directly. 'Originally there is no distinction of suffering and joy' reveals the transcendence of error and the negation of the false. For if the purity and impurity of the four lands are spoken of: in the Saha of cohabitation there is only suffering and no joy, while in Qingtai there is only joy and no suffering. Comparing Expedient with cohabitation, cohabitation has only suffering and Expedient only joy. Taking Expedient in its own land, its impure region has only suffering and its pure region only joy. Comparing Real Reward with Expedient, Expedient has only suffering and Real Reward only joy. Taking Real Reward in its own land, its impure region has only suffering and its pure region only joy. Comparing Real Reward with Still-Light, Real Reward has only suffering and Still-Light only joy. Taking Still-Light in its own land, its impure region has only suffering and its pure region only joy. All of the foregoing is spoken in terms of what is accomplished through cultivation—non-dual yet dual—and so there is the distinction of suffering and joy. But the preface's words 'originally there is no distinction of suffering and joy' refer to the nature endowed with the ten realms: those aggregates and lands have only the fused nature of the suffering and joy of the ten realms, and not the differentiated characteristics of the suffering and joy of the ten realms. That is, the unchanging suchness equally possessed by living beings and Buddhas, which originally has no distinction of purity and impurity—how could there be a difference of suffering and joy? Hence this single phrase is sectioned as 'the true source is non-dual,' serving as the basis for the following 'delusive streams produce distinctions.' This is what the Surangama Sutra calls 'the nature-consciousness is subtle and bright, the original consciousness is bright and subtle,' and again, 'pure and of itself so, pervading the dharma-realm.' The four kinds of Pure Land are given in full below.
[Commentary] Delusive consciousness, in its teeming confusion, then brings about the difference of sages and ordinary beings.

[Sub-commentary] 'Delusive consciousness' is the collective name for the three delusions. For living beings, from beginningless time, within the subtle brightness of the nature-consciousness and the bright subtlety of the original consciousness, a single thought suddenly darkened, and falsely made a shining awareness. Because of awareness a locus was set up; the locus having been falsely set, false capacity arose. Within the undifferentiated, blazingly it became differentiated, serving as the three subtle marks; and then ignorance and dust-like delusion served as the six coarse marks. The views and thoughts, in the first transformation, became the impure Still-Light; in the second, the impure Real Reward; in the third, the impure Expedient; in the fourth, the impure cohabitation. Thus they became bodhisattvas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, and beings of the six realms. Hence it is said, 'Delusive consciousness in its teeming confusion then brings about the difference of sages and ordinary beings.' This is what the Surangama Sutra calls 'following the minds of beings, as their measuring capacity'; and what the Avatamsaka Sutra means by 'able to follow the conditions of purity and defilement, thereby dividing the ten dharma-realms.' For this reason it is sectioned as 'delusive streams produce distinctions.' One must further understand that though the first line says 'the Still-Light is truly pure, originally free of the distinction of suffering and joy,' it does not preclude non-distinction yet distinction—that is, the nature endowed with the ten realms. And though the second line says 'delusive consciousness in its teeming confusion then brings about the difference of sages and ordinary beings,' it does not preclude distinction yet non-distinction—that is, that within the nature there is no difference. This is precisely because, though suchness is unchanging, it does not preclude its changing yet following conditions; and though delusive consciousness follows conditions, it does not preclude its following conditions yet remaining unchanging. Because of the conditions of conditions, therefore, there is non-distinction yet distinction; because of the unchanging, there is distinction yet non-distinction. One who can understand this is able to grasp that this thought of Buddha-recitation is the whole nature arising to bring about pure practice, and the whole practice being gathered within the one nature.

blocks.text: Next, the actual account of the rise of the occasion.

inline.s: [Commentary] Therefore, drifting through the five turbidities and unable to return to the one true, our Shakyamuni manifested birth in the world of endurance.

[Sub-commentary] This is the actual account of the rise of the occasion for the Tathagata's preaching of the sutra. The Tathagata had long realized the true and constant, so why should he have been born into a king's palace? It was solely because all living beings, from beginningless time, had fallen, that there was this appearing in the Saha world. 'Drifting through the five turbidities' means that living beings, from beginningless time, from the ocean of the nirvana nature roused the waves of consciousness, obscuring the perfect clarity and losing the serene depth, muddying the bright subtlety and drowning the true nature. This is because first they lost it through movement—hence 'drifting.' This is what the Surangama Sutra means by 'the bright awareness and the empty darkness, mutually dependent, give rise to agitation.' Next they lost it through dullness—hence the 'five turbidities,' which the Surangama Sutra calls 'darkness obscured becoming emptiness.' Yet dullness must contain movement, and movement must contain dullness; thus drifting is turbidity, and turbidity is drifting. Once the delusion of dullness and movement has taken form, the truth of brightness and stillness is lost. Only these five turbidities differ as coarse and fine. As the Surangama Sutra says of the turbidity of the kalpa: 'You see empty space pervading the ten directions; space and sight are not separated. There is emptiness without a substance; there is sight without awareness. Woven together, falsehood is formed; this is the first, called the turbidity of the kalpa.' This speaks together of the three delusions. If, as the ordinary explanation has it, only when human life was twenty thousand years did one enter the turbidity of the kalpa, that singles out the two delusions of views and thoughts at their most blazing. And yet there may be the fine without the coarse, but never the coarse without the fine. Now this points directly to the time of Shakyamuni's manifest birth in the world of endurance, when the coarse suited the capacity. If it says 'unable to return to the one true,' that too speaks together with the fine. The manifestation of birth in the world of endurance is precisely the response of descending—the impure cohabitation land of ordinary beings and sages, spoken of merely as the humble response of a sixteen-foot aged monk's body and appearance. If the fine delusions are also included, the meaning embraces the response descending into the upper two lands.

blocks.text: Next, the exposition of the sutra is divided into two: first, the account of the place and the capacities; second, the account of the essential teaching. Now first, the account of the place and capacities.

inline.s: [Commentary] At the auspicious gathering in the Jeta Grove he addressed the sharp faculties of Shariputra.

[Sub-commentary] The auspicious gathering in the Jeta Grove is the place where the sutra was preached; Shariputra, of sharp faculties, is the one whose capacity was met. In discussing the capacities to which this sutra is addressed, there are three grades: first, bodhisattvas; second, the two vehicles; third, ordinary beings. For the Pure Land teaching the various lesser-vehicle sutras do not speak of at all, since once the fruits and the effects have been exhausted the body is extinguished and consciousness destroyed, and nothing is said of birth after death. Now this is spoken at length, and it is a bodhisattva teaching. If one traces its origin, the sutra was preached in the Vaipulya [Expanded] period, precisely at the time of refuting the one-sided and censuring the lesser, extolling the greater and extolling the Round. Censuring the lesser vehicles, who are not reborn outside the realms, it says 'there is birth,' and especially points to that land as having immeasurable, unbounded shravaka disciples; and it praises to the utmost the subtle, wonderful adornments of that land's retribution-body and environment. Thus the extolling of the greater and the extolling of the Round are lodged within it. Moreover, Sariputra was foremost among the many disciples, so he addressed him, causing him to turn from the lesser to the greater. As for the capacities directly aimed at, they are those in the ordinary state; holding the name for seven days with a single minded, unconfused heart, they immediately attain rebirth; and once they have entered that auspicious assembly they attain non-retrogression. Viewed thus, though these are ordinary beings, the teaching belongs to the Round and to the Sudden, as is also to be known.
